title: Heaps
summary: Peek the extreme in O(1) and fix the heap in O(log n), stored as an array.

parts.rule: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array where each parent is ordered against its children. In a min-heap every parent is less than or equal to its children. Peek the extreme in O(1). Push and pop restore the heap in O(log n) by sift-up or sift-down. Child indices of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2; parent is (i-1)//2.
parts.why: Top-k and "always take the smallest available" problems are heap-shaped. Candidates re-sort the whole array on every change or scan for the minimum in linear time per extraction. Saying peek is constant and extract is logarithmic is the cost story interviewers expect.
parts.example: Build a min-heap by inserting 5, 3, 8, 1. Start with [5]. Insert 3: append to get [5, 3], sift up by swapping with parent → [3, 5]. Insert 8 → [3, 5, 8]; eight stays. Insert 1 → [3, 5, 8, 1]; sift one past five → [3, 1, 8, 5], then past three → [1, 3, 8, 5]. Peek returns 1. Pop the minimum: move the last value five to the root → [5, 3, 8], then sift down by swapping with the smaller child three → [3, 5, 8]. For the two largest values in [4, 1, 7, 3], keep a min-heap of size two; after processing all elements the heap holds 4 and 7.
parts.use: Use a heap for top-k, next-distance selection in Dijkstra-style loops, scheduling the earliest event, and merging k sorted lists by always taking the current smallest head. Use a max-heap when the extreme you need is the largest value.
parts.refuse: Refuse a heap when you need arbitrary decrease-key without an index handle — a plain binary heap makes that awkward. Refuse heapsorting if a library sort is enough and you do not need online extracts. Refuse claiming constant-time delete of an arbitrary interior value. Refuse treating heap order as left-to-right sorted order; inorder of a heap is not sorted.

body:
Rule. A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array where each parent is ordered against its children. In a min-heap every parent is less than or equal to its children. Peek the extreme in O(1). Push and pop restore the heap in O(log n) by sift-up or sift-down. Child indices of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2; parent is (i-1)//2.

Why it matters. Top-k and "always take the smallest available" problems are heap-shaped. Candidates re-sort the whole array on every change or scan for the minimum in linear time per extraction. Saying peek is constant and extract is logarithmic is the cost story interviewers expect.

Worked example. Build a min-heap by inserting 5, 3, 8, 1. Start with [5]. Insert 3: append to get [5, 3], sift up by swapping with parent → [3, 5]. Insert 8 → [3, 5, 8]; eight stays. Insert 1 → [3, 5, 8, 1]; sift one past five → [3, 1, 8, 5], then past three → [1, 3, 8, 5]. Peek returns 1. Pop the minimum: move the last value five to the root → [5, 3, 8], then sift down by swapping with the smaller child three → [3, 5, 8]. For the two largest values in [4, 1, 7, 3], keep a min-heap of size two; after processing all elements the heap holds 4 and 7.

[[diagram:heap-array]]

When to use. Use a heap for top-k, next-distance selection in Dijkstra-style loops, scheduling the earliest event, and merging k sorted lists by always taking the current smallest head. Use a max-heap when the extreme you need is the largest value.

When to refuse. Refuse a heap when you need arbitrary decrease-key without an index handle — a plain binary heap makes that awkward. Refuse heapsorting if a library sort is enough and you do not need online extracts. Refuse claiming constant-time delete of an arbitrary interior value. Refuse treating heap order as left-to-right sorted order; inorder of a heap is not sorted.
